claims.text: The starting alloy is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
As-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is a simple, single-phase solid solution.
As-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
As-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has good ductility and machinability.
High local lattice distortion facilitates dislocation glide in the untreated CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Dynamic recovery accompanies dislocation glide in untreated CoCrFeNiTi.
Efficient dislocation glide and dynamic recovery cause the alloy's relatively low hardness and strength while preserving high plasticity.
A controlled heat treatment can induce nanoscale chemical ordering or fine precipitation in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi without a major compositional change.
Nanoscale chemically ordered regions or fine precipitates act as dislocation-pinning sites.
The added obstacles to dislocation motion will increase yield strength and hardness relative to the as-cast alloy.
The strength and hardness increases will occur at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
The modified alloy will retain acceptable ductility, potentially with only a small ductility trade-off.
The baseline alloy is defect-rich as well as single-phase.
The hypothesis is limited to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested from 25 °C to 600 °C under quasi-static loading.
The treatment is limited to conditions that produce nanoscale ordering without causing a full phase change.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on the precise heat-treatment or compositional-modification parameters.
An overly aggressive microstructural modification may cause brittleness.
A controlled comparison can use identically composed as-cast and heat-treated samples, with TEM or APT used to verify nanoscale heterogeneities before mechanical testing.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase after verified formation of the proposed heterogeneities would falsify the predicted strengthening effect.
Failure of the treatment to produce the anticipated nanoscale heterogeneities would itself falsify the proposed strengthening mechanism.

contradictions.description: The intervention allows a 'minor compositional tweak' while saying that overall elemental ratios do not change, whereas the boundary and controlled experiment require equimolar, identically composed samples. A compositional tweak necessarily changes at least one elemental ratio unless no actual composition change is made.

The hypothesis permits formation of fine precipitates but simultaneously requires maintenance of a single-phase solid solution and no full phase change. Distinct precipitates ordinarily constitute an additional phase; chemical ordering without precipitation could satisfy the single-phase restriction, but precipitation cannot.
